Chapter 7: Adapting to Change—Embracing the Unknown
Change—it's one of the few things in life we can really count on, isn’t it? But let’s be honest, it almost never shows up when we want it to, or the way we expect. For a lot of us, the very idea of change feels unsettling. It can stir up anxiety, that uneasy sense of losing our grip, like the world’s shifting under our feet and we’re not sure where we’ll land.
But here’s what she learned, after years of facing the unexpected: adapting to change isn’t about holding on for dear life. It’s about learning to let go—gently, even gracefully.
She often thought back to the day her longtime home was sold. That house was more than just walls and a roof; it was filled with memories, laughter, the echoes of so many moments. Packing up felt like closing a chapter she just wasn’t ready to end. But once she moved and settled into a new place, something surprising happened. She found unexpected gifts—like a neighbor who quickly became a close friend, or a garden that bloomed in ways she’d never imagined before. It was a reminder that every ending holds the seeds for a new beginning, if we’re willing to notice.
At work, she’d seen how entire organizations and communities wrestle with change too. New policies, new leaders, shifting expectations—each one brought its own set of challenges. Some folks hung back, clinging to old routines because, well, that’s just what they knew. Others leaned in, got creative, and discovered new strengths they didn’t realize they had. She noticed something important: the people who thrived weren’t always the most talented. They were the most flexible—the ones willing to learn, to listen, and to give it another try when things didn’t go as planned.
Change on a personal level? That called for a different kind of bravery. Health issues, losing someone you love, or just the slow changes that come with getting older—these all forced her to rethink what was possible. Of course there were tough days, moments spent grieving what was gone. But she found comfort in the routines that stuck around—a morning walk, a favorite song, the steady rhythm of prayer. Over time, she discovered something powerful. She could get through anything, not because she was unbreakable, but because she’d learned how to bend.
Most people, she realized, spend a lot of energy fighting change, hoping that things will just stay the same. But what if, instead, we chose to meet the unknown with curiosity? What if we leaned in and adapted, even just a little? That’s when you discover a kind of resilience that can carry you through anything life throws your way.
